It's the same reason why it seems like ordering a 12 inch pizza instead of an 8 inch pizza isn't a huge increase, but in reality it's more than twice as much food.

Our brains process numbers logarithmically, meaning, they care more about the proportional difference between numbers than about the actual difference. This can play tricks on our perception because things that are significantly bigger than other things often look pretty close in size. A 200 pound person is in fact twice as much raw human as a 100 pound person, but might look only maybe a head taller.
Well, an 8 inch pizza has an area of 16π, while a 12 inch pizza has an area of 36π. So the 12 inch has 36/16, or 2.25, times more pizza than the 8 inch.
All I know now is that I want pizza.

Logarithmic scaling works based on proportional differences. If you have 3 items and you gave one away your brain would register it as "Holy shit, we just gave one third of those things away, that's a lot!" but if you had 30 of those items and gave 3 away your brain would say "3 out of 30 isn't all that much, no problem". In real numbers though you actually gave away three times as many items in the second example, it just didn't seem like it, because your brain fixed it's notion of what is "a lot" based proportionally to how many you had.

People get messed up by this a lot, especially when buying things. Someone might say "Does it really matter if I sell my house for 340k instead of 350k? It's not that big a difference right?" Actually, that's $10.000 god damn dollars. It's a big freaking difference. Our tendency to look at whether something is a lot or a little as a matter of proportions can lead us astray very easily. Same goes for why people spend too much money right after cashing a paycheck. Spending 100 bucks right after you got payed doesn't seem like a lot, but in reality those 100 bucks are worth just as much while you are flush as they are when you're broke. Your brain just registers them proportionally to how much money you currently have, so it can seem like a minor expense or it can seem like a huge sum.

Of course the reason our brain works that way is because in nature proportions are more important than numbers. If your tribe is fighting another tribe and they outnumber you by 10 guys it's much more important how big of a portion of their army 10 guys is than whether or not that number is exactly 10. In a fight 1000 vs 1010 it's not really important, but in a fight of 10 vs 20 it's a huge difference.

Why King Kong's existence can't be explained by the simple body size scaling of a gorilla, all other things being equal.
